Hi everyone! I’m a high school student from Türkiye with a strong passion for aerospace engineering, astronomy, space exploration, and technology. My goal is to pursue aerospace engineering and contribute to the future of space exploration.

I’m particularly interested in solving real-world challenges through creativity, scientific research, and innovative thinking. I enjoy collaborating with motivated people, exploring new ideas, and turning ambitious concepts into meaningful projects
summary: Lunar Landing Navigator is a web app that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. For any site and landing time, it shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real terrain horizon. That tells you when solar power is available and when direct-to-Earth communication is possible, and how long until the next sunset or Earthset. Its What If? simulator shows instantly what a launch delay, a site change or a longer mission does to those windows. It turns NASA ephemeris and topography data into clear visuals, without the complexity of expert tools.
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Landing Navigator is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. You pick a site, either from 16 curated locations (Apollo 11–17, CLPS and commercial missions such as IM-1 and IM-2, international missions such as Chandrayaan-3 and Chang'e 6, and south-polar craters) or any custom coordinate. Then you choose a landing time and mission length. The app shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real horizon at that site:

  • how high the Sun is (a proxy for solar power)
  • whether Earth is visible for direct-to-Earth communication
  • how long until the next sunset or Earthset
  • the longest periods of darkness and communication blackout

Under the hood:

  • Ephemeris: Sun and Earth positions are calculated in the browser with published astronomical models (Meeus; IAU 2009 lunar rotation), including the Moon's libration. We validated them against NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441): they agree to better than 0.01°. The app can also query Horizons live.
  • Terrain: the horizon around each site is traced over NASA LRO LOLA topography, out to 200 km and including lunar curvature. There is no atmospheric refraction, because the Moon has no atmosphere.
  • Shadow map: a background worker ray-traces a live shadow map of the south pole for the selected moment.

Key features:

  • What If? Mission Simulator: shows instantly how a delay of 1–30 days, a site change or a longer mission changes the windows. For example, a one-week slip at Mons Mouton cuts sunlight from 100% to 56% and adds six days of darkness.
  • Best-lit spot search: scans the terrain around a site for better ground. From Shackleton's permanently dark floor, it finds a fully sunlit rim point 10 km away.
  • Site comparison: up to three sites side by side.
  • Landing-window scan: covers 30 days up to a full year, so it captures both lunar days and seasons.

Benefits

  • Speed: a question that normally means working through several expert tools (Horizons, QuickMap, Moon Trek) and raw data takes seconds.
  • Terrain realism: with LOLA terrain, four known permanently shadowed craters correctly stay dark all year. A smooth-sphere model wrongly puts them in sunlight about half the time.
  • Transparency: every number is labelled SOURCED, LOLA-DERIVED, COMPUTED or ILLUSTRATIVE, so users know what to trust.
  • Accessibility: it runs in any browser with no installation. A shareable link reproduces any scenario, and results can be exported as CSV or JSON.

Intended impact

  • Mission planners: when hardware or launch schedules shift, they can re-evaluate dates and alternative sites in the same region immediately.
  • Science and engineering teams: a shared, visual picture of power and communication constraints.
  • Educators and the public: an intuitive way to see why the lunar south pole is so hard to explore. A Learn mode explains libration, terrain shadows and the missing atmosphere, and a Moon-vs-Earth comparison shows how extreme lunar conditions are.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (React Three Fiber) for the 3D Moon, Recharts for charts, and Web Workers for ray tracing. Python with NumPy processes the LOLA data.
  • Hosting: GitHub with GitHub Pages, deployed automatically by GitHub Actions.
  • Data: NASA/JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA topography (PDS Geosciences Node), the NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit, NASA NSSDC and LROC site coordinates.
  • Hardware: none beyond a standard laptop.
  • AI assistance: the project was developed with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude by Anthropic). The app itself contains no AI.

Creativity

  • One interface for three data views: a 3D globe lit by the real Sun, a panorama of the horizon as an astronaut would see it, and a ray-traced shadow map that animates as time passes.
  • Planning moves, not just data: "what if we slip a week?", "where is better ground nearby?" and "when is the best window this year?" each take a single click.
  • Plain language: the simulator writes a plain-language impact summary instead of only printing numbers.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific integrity: we never invent NASA measurements. Site coordinates come from cited sources, results are tested against NASA references, and terrain resolution and coverage limits are stated in the app.
  • Honest framing: illumination is presented as a power-availability proxy, not a power forecast. Earth visibility is necessary but not sufficient for communication, because ground-station scheduling is not modelled. The planning score is a transparent heuristic, not an official NASA determination.
  • Usability for mixed audiences: technical detail for planners, plus explanations for students.
  • Design: a consistent colour language (gold for sunlight, cyan for Earth, red for risk).
  • Performance: heavy calculations run in the background.
  • Access: the app works offline on its built-in model, and on phones and desktops.
